title: Governor of Tennessee

context.text: Open seat: Republican Gov. Bill Lee is term-limited and cannot seek a third consecutive term.
Republican primary (Aug. 6): U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn won with about 44% of the vote, ahead of U.S. Rep. John Rose (about 33%) and state Rep. Monty Fritts (about 24%).
Democratic primary (Aug. 6): Memphis City Council member Jerri Green won with about 69% of the vote, ahead of Carnita Atwater (about 18%) and three other candidates.

Thirteen independents qualified for the November ballot by petition, making 15 governor candidates in total. They are listed by WSMV and the Nashville Banner voter guide, and the Tennessee Firefly reports the same count from the Secretary of State's qualifier list.

candidates.name: Marsha Blackburn
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Aug. 6 Republican primary with about 44% of the vote.

summary.text: Marsha Blackburn is a U.S. Senator from Tennessee, serving since 2019, and the Republican nominee for governor. She previously served in the Tennessee Senate and for sixteen years in the U.S. House.

background.text: Grew up in Laurel, Mississippi; graduated from Mississippi State University (B.S. in home economics, 1974) on a 4-H scholarship.
Executive director of the Tennessee Film, Entertainment, and Music Commission beginning in 1995; served in the Tennessee Senate from 1999 to 2003.
Led a statewide campaign against a proposed state income tax while in the Tennessee Senate.
Represented Tennessee in the U.S. House from 2003 to 2019, then was elected to the U.S. Senate.

priorities.text: Keeping taxes low and growing the economy, building on her opposition to a state income tax.
Immigration enforcement: supporting mass deportations and keeping sanctuary cities out of Tennessee.
Parental rights and school choice, including fully implementing Tennessee's new school choice law.
Keeping men out of girls' and women's sports.

positions.summary: Her campaign says she is 100 percent pro-life and has supported legislation to help end federal funding of abortion.
Says she backs President Trump's immigration policy and mass deportations, and will ensure sanctuary cities never have a home in Tennessee.
positions.quote: Marsha backs President Trump's immigration policy 100 percent

positions.summary: Says she supports school choice and will fully implement Tennessee's new school choice law.
Says she introduced legislation to block rules that would let biological males compete in women's sports and will make sure girls' sports are protected.

record.text: Voted yes on the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which passed the Senate 64–35.
Voted yes on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) in the Senate, which passed 50–50 with the Vice President breaking the tie.
Voted yes on the GENIUS Act (S. 1582), a stablecoin regulation bill that passed the Senate 68–30.

candidates.name: Jerri Green
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Aug. 6 Democratic primary with about 69% of the vote.

summary.text: Jerri Green is a member of the Memphis City Council representing District 2 and the Democratic nominee for governor. She is an attorney and former public defender and executive director of the Community Legal Center.

background.text: Raised in Memphis; B.A. in English and political science from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and J.D. from Georgetown University Law Center.
Began her career as a juvenile public defender in Nashville; later executive director of the Community Legal Center in Memphis.
Served Shelby County Mayor Lee Harris as senior policy advisor and deputy chief of staff before joining the Memphis City Council in 2024.

priorities.text: Day-one actions using federal TANF funds: waiving security deposits, clearing the child care waitlist and erasing medical debt.
Expanding Medicaid, protecting TennCare, and repealing Tennessee's near-total abortion ban.
Fully funding public schools rather than 'unaccountable voucher schemes', raising teacher pay and expanding universal pre-K.
Gun safety measures including universal background checks and red flag laws.

positions.summary: Platform says she would repeal Tennessee's near-total abortion ban and sign an executive order protecting doctors from prosecution.
Platform calls for universal background checks on all gun sales, red flag laws, closing domestic violence loopholes and free gun locks.
Would sign an executive order on day one to end Tennessee Highway Patrol and law enforcement cooperation with ICE and ban ICE from state buildings.
Would expand Medicaid to cover more working families, keep rural hospitals open and protect TennCare.
Platform says she would fully fund K-12 public education 'not siphon dollars into unaccountable voucher schemes'.
Day-one plan uses $50 million of TANF funds to clear the child care waitlist; platform also proposes universal pre-K and more affordable child care.
Platform calls for investing in renewable energy and green jobs and enforcing clean air and water standards.

record.text: Sponsored Memphis Ordinance No. 5906 to let the City Court Clerk's office accept partial payments for traffic citations; it was approved on second reading.

Her campaign site says she launched Tennessee's first free gun lock-by-mail program in Memphis and led an effort to clear $17 million in medical debt for 12,000 Memphians (campaign claims, not independently verified).

summary.text: David Hatley is an independent candidate for governor and a businessman from Gray in Washington County. He says he has built nine companies and a hot tub manufacturing plant in East Tennessee. A mid-September TargetSmart poll of 600 likely voters, reported by the Nashville Banner, showed him at 10%; the poll was paid for by a PAC that has funded Democratic nominee Jerri Green's campaign.

background.text: Entrepreneur from Elizabethton; his campaign says he built nine companies, holds patents and created about 750 Tennessee jobs (campaign figures, not independently verified).

priorities.text: Education is one of five priorities on his campaign site, including expert reading coaches in the state's 100 lowest-performing elementary schools, trade education and apprenticeships, and higher teacher pay.

summary.text: Lauren Pinkston is an independent candidate for governor from Columbia and a former assistant professor at Lipscomb University. She began as a public school teacher, holds a doctorate from Clemson University and has started businesses employing survivors of human trafficking; this is her first campaign.

Misam Abidi of Nolensville is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition. His campaign site describes past work as a personal banker, and his platform pillars include crypto innovation, a proposed Tennessee Dividend Fund and a Tennessee Skills Guarantee.

background.text: Allegation, not a conviction: on June 12, 2026 the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Tennessee announced an 11-count federal indictment of Misam M. Abidi (three counts of wire fraud, two of operating an unlicensed money transmitting business, three of aiding in the preparation of false tax returns and three of money laundering) over his cryptocurrency investment firm Star Credit Holdings, alleging he diverted over $1.9 million of investor funds. WREG and WSMV report that he is the independent candidate for governor. Charges are allegations; the guide found no report of a verdict.

summary.text: Dean Brewer of Knoxville is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition. No occupation or biographical detail could be sourced.
Edgar 'Ray' Brown of Oliver Springs is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition and is listed as an electrician.
Wendell Jackson of Clarksville is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition and is listed as a spoken word performer and comedian.
Charles Van Morgan of Knoxville is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition and is listed as a businessman and former police officer.

Eddie Lee Murphy of Spring Hill is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition. He was one of eight Republican candidates in the October 2025 special election for Tennessee's 7th Congressional District.

Victor L. Scoggin of Pegram is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition. His campaign site describes him as a Navy veteran, retired volunteer firefighter and farmer and founder of Save the Cumberland Inc.
Dave Seeman of Nashville is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition. His campaign site describes him as an engineer and small business owner.
Karl Knox Smithson of McMinnville is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition and is listed as a homeless community activist.
L. Webb Taylor of Memphis is an independent candidate for governor who qualified by petition and is listed as a corporate health and wellness consultant.
Robert C. Vick is an independent candidate for governor and a longtime East Tennessee educator who qualified by petition.

researchNotes: Ballotpedia and the Tennessee Secretary of State candidate-list PDF were blocked, so the 15-candidate slate was checked against three independent news lists that agree exactly (WSMV Oct. 14, Nashville Banner voter guide, WSMV Sept. 28 candidate guide) and The Tennessee Firefly's candidate pages (which cite the Secretary of State's certified list). Blackburn's positions are from her campaign issue pages and Green's from her campaign platform; only positions with direct sources are listed. Federal key votes for Blackburn are expected to be added by script. Hatley is listed at the basic tier because a September 2026 TargetSmart poll reported by the Nashville Banner showed him at 10%. Minimal-tier summaries for independents rely on The Tennessee Firefly (which draws on Politics1, campaign sites and Ballotpedia) because Ballotpedia could not be read; occupation descriptions that the Firefly could not corroborate are stated as 'listed as'. Primary-result percentages come from Wikipedia's results tables.
